mcqs.question: In the back-of-envelope estimate, why does 1M concurrent viewers matter more for read-path capacity than 100K daily uploads matter for write-path capacity?
options: Concurrent egress (viewers x average bitrate) produces a sustained multi-terabit number that immediately rules out serving from origin storage alone
Uploads never need to be transcoded, only stored, so they place no load anywhere
The metadata database can only handle read traffic, never write traffic
Concurrent viewers only affect storage cost, not network throughput
mcqs.explanation: 1M viewers x ~3Mbps is roughly 3Tbps of sustained egress — a number that has to be served from edge caches, not origin. Uploads absolutely get transcoded (that's most of the write-path cost); the metadata DB handles both reads and writes; and concurrent viewers is fundamentally a network throughput problem, not just a storage one.

mcqs.question: What two live signals does a player's adaptive bitrate (ABR) logic primarily use to pick the next chunk's quality?
options: The video's total file size and its upload date
How much video is buffered ahead, and the measured download throughput of recent chunks
The viewer's account subscription tier only
The resolution of the device's screen, fixed for the whole session
mcqs.explanation: ABR reacts to real-time buffer health and measured throughput so it can step down before a stall or step up when bandwidth allows. Screen resolution can bound the ceiling but isn't the primary adaptive signal; file size and upload date are static and irrelevant to live network conditions.

mcqs.question: A platform expects most uploaded videos to be watched thousands of times. Which rendition strategy fits that access pattern best?
options: On-the-fly transcoding for every playback request
No transcoding at all — serve the original upload directly
Precomputed renditions generated once at upload time
Transcoding only when a viewer explicitly requests a resolution change mid-playback
mcqs.explanation: Precomputing pays the transcode cost once per video and amortizes it across thousands of views, which is exactly right when view count is high. On-the-fly transcoding repeats that cost per view, wasting compute at scale. Serving the raw original skips ABR entirely, and transcoding only on resolution-change requests still means live, per-viewer encode latency.

mcqs.question: Why should the transcode worker pool autoscale against queue depth rather than upload rate?
options: Upload rate is impossible to measure reliably
Queue depth is cheaper to compute than upload rate
Autoscaling on upload rate is not supported by any cloud provider
Queue depth reflects the actual backlog even if per-job time has silently increased, while upload rate alone can look normal while a backlog grows
mcqs.explanation: Queue depth directly reflects unprocessed backlog, even when a slowdown in per-job time (not upload volume) is the real cause. A steady upload rate can mask a growing backlog if jobs are silently taking longer. Upload rate is easy enough to measure and autoscaling on it is a policy choice rather than a provider limitation — this option is the deliberate distractor, since it names the wrong metric as if it were disqualifying.

mcqs.question: Why is gating a video's publish on the completion of every rendition in the ladder (including the highest resolution) usually the wrong design?
options: High-resolution transcodes are technically impossible to complete quickly at any scale
It blows the time-to-first-playback SLA for all viewers, even though most early viewers wouldn't select the highest rendition anyway
Only the lowest rendition is ever actually watched, so higher renditions are pointless to produce at all
Players cannot handle a video gaining new renditions after playback has already started
mcqs.explanation: The highest rendition is typically the slowest to transcode, so waiting on it delays every viewer's first playback for no benefit — especially since most early viewers are on devices that wouldn't request 4K immediately. High renditions are producible, just slower; higher renditions do get watched over a video's lifetime; and ABR players are designed to tolerate a manifest gaining renditions mid-life.
